name: How do I know if my old cabinets are good enough to reface instead of replace?

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my old cabinets are good enough to reface instead of replace?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Yes—cabinet refacing can be a strong choice when the existing cabinet boxes are square, dry, securely attached, and laid out in a way that already works. The service typically updates exposed cabinet surfaces while replacing doors, drawer fronts, and hardware, rather than removing the cabinet boxes.

Context: This approach can refresh an outdated kitchen without committing to a full cabinet tear-out. It is less suitable when storage, cabinet locations, or the overall kitchen layout must change.

Key factors:
- Inspect boxes for swelling, delamination, water damage, sagging, and loose joints.
- Confirm the current layout supports your appliances, storage needs, and countertop plans.
- Compare veneer, laminate, painted finishes, door profiles, and hardware before choosing.

Practical guidance: Photograph every cabinet interior, note damage near sinks and dishwashers, and ask Elite Remodeling & Design to evaluate the boxes before discussing finishes. A design consultation can also reveal whether refacing alone solves the functional problems.

Elite Remodeling & Design can coordinate cabinet decisions with broader kitchen remodeling work when the project involves countertops, lighting, plumbing, or layout changes.
acceptedAnswer.description: Refacing works when cabinet boxes are structurally sound, dry, securely attached, and arranged in a usable layout. Replacement is usually more appropriate for swollen particleboard, water damage, sagging boxes, or a kitchen that needs a new footprint. Have the boxes inspected before selecting doors and finishes.
